title: Maximum Element-Sum of a Complete Subset of Indices
statement: Number the positions of the integer array `nums` from 1 to `n` (1-indexed). A set of positions is called complete when, for any two positions `i` and `j` in it, the product `i * j` is a perfect square; a set with a single position is always complete. Return the largest value of `nums[i]` summed over all positions `i` of some complete set.
notes:
## Intuition

Split every position into a square-free part times a perfect square: `18 = 2 * 3²`, `12 = 3 * 2²`. Two positions multiply to a perfect square exactly when their square-free parts match, because the squares contribute even exponents and the square-free parts must cancel each other's odd primes. So the complete sets are the groups `core * 1², core * 2², core * 3², ...` (and their subsets). Since every value is positive, the best set is a whole group. Testing every subset would cost O(2ⁿ).

## Approach

1. For each `core` from 1 to `n`, start `sum` at 0.
2. For `root = 1, 2, 3, ...` while `core * root * root <= n`, add `nums` at that 1-based position.
3. Keep the largest `sum` in `best` and return it.

A `core` that is not square-free (such as 4) only rebuilds part of a real group, which is still complete and never beats the full group, so no factorisation is needed.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [8, 7, 3, 5, 7, 2, 4, 9]`, `n = 8`. For `core = 1` the positions are 1 and 4, giving `8 + 5 = 13`, so `best = 13`. For `core = 2` the positions are 2 and 8 (`2 * 2² = 8`), giving `7 + 9 = 16`, so `best = 16`. Every `core` from 3 to 8 fits only `root = 1`, giving single values 3, 5, 7, 2, 4 and 9, none above 16. The answer is `16`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `core` visits about `sqrt(n / core)` positions, and those counts add up to roughly `2n`.
- Space: O(1): just the running sums.

## Pitfalls

- Positions are 1-based; read `nums[core * root * root - 1]`.
- The square condition is about positions, not the values stored there.
- Sums reach about `10^13`, so Java and C need a 64-bit total.
- Grouping only with position 1 (the perfect squares) misses sets like `{2, 8, 18}`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `core` | the shared square-free factor of one group of positions |
| `root` | which square multiplies `core` to give the next position |
| `sum` | total of the values in the current group |
| `best` | largest group total found so far |

narration.3: best holds the largest complete-set total seen so far.
narration.5: Try each possible shared factor; the positions core, 4·core, 9·core... form a complete set.
narration.6: Start this group's total at zero.
narration.7: Step through core times 1², 2², 3²... while the position stays inside the array.
narration.8: Add the value at that 1-based position.
narration.10: Keep the larger of this group's total and the best so far.
narration.12: Every group has been tried; return the best total.
